polynomial.title: Can a squared size make the rule bend?
polynomial.label: Shape of the rule
polynomial.help: A straight-line model uses size. A curved model can also use size × size. Both are fitted to the same houses, so their learned coefficients and baselines can differ. Compare the shapes and the predictions.
polynomial.fixed: Keep the training houses and new house-size index 2 fixed. These are two previously fitted models, not a change to one coefficient.

options.label: Curve: use size and squared size

polynomial.title: What if size and room count work together?
polynomial.label: Measurements the model can use
polynomial.help: An interaction multiplies two inputs so the effect of one can depend on the other. Let a describe size and b describe rooms. These are simplified indices: a=2 and b=3, so their interaction is 2 × 3 = 6.
polynomial.fixed: Keep the inputs [2,3] and baseline 1 fixed. The original size and room coefficients stay 2 and 1. Extra columns use supplied coefficients; these two rules are illustrations, not fitted models.

options.label: Also use squares and size × rooms

polynomial.title: Does a more flexible curve predict new houses better?
polynomial.label: Curve complexity
polynomial.help: Degree is the highest input power. A higher degree can bend more. Check the error on training houses and on separate development houses.
polynomial.fixed: Use the same houses, query size 0.4, and no coefficient penalty. Development error guides selection.

polynomial.title: Can we trust the curve outside the sizes it has seen?
polynomial.label: House-size index
polynomial.help: Interpolation means predicting inside the observed range. Extrapolation means going beyond it. A numerical answer alone does not establish reliability.
polynomial.fixed: Keep the degree-3 model fixed; training sizes span −1 to 1.

regularization.title: Can a penalty restrain the model?
regularization.label: Penalty strength (alpha)
regularization.help: Alpha controls how much large coefficients are discouraged. Larger values apply a stronger penalty. Watch the coefficients and held-out error; stronger is not always better.
regularization.fixed: Use the same housing rows, model family and training-only scaling.

regularization.title: How strongly should Ridge shrink coefficients?
regularization.label: Penalty strength (alpha)
regularization.help: Alpha controls how much large coefficients are discouraged. Larger values apply a stronger penalty. Watch the coefficients and held-out error; stronger is not always better.
regularization.fixed: Use the same housing rows, model family and training-only scaling.

regularization.title: Can Lasso set a coefficient to zero?
regularization.label: Penalty strength (alpha)
regularization.help: Alpha controls how much large coefficients are discouraged. Larger values apply a stronger penalty. Watch the coefficients and held-out error; stronger is not always better.
regularization.fixed: Use the same housing rows, model family and training-only scaling.

regularization.title: How does Elastic Net combine two penalties?
regularization.label: Share of the Lasso penalty
regularization.help: Elastic Net mixes Ridge shrinkage with Lasso sparsity. Raising this share moves the mixture toward Lasso; total penalty strength stays fixed.
regularization.fixed: Keep alpha at 0.1 and use the same housing data.

regularization.title: Which rows may teach the scaler?
regularization.label: Rows used to learn scaling
regularization.help: A scaler learns averages and spreads. Letting it inspect validation rows leaks information into the workflow before the model is evaluated.
regularization.fixed: Keep the model, penalty and housing data fixed.

regularization.title: Does a smaller coefficient make a better prediction?
regularization.label: Penalty strength
regularization.help: Compare prediction error as well as coefficient size. A small coefficient is a model result, not proof that a feature has no real-world effect.
regularization.fixed: Keep the penalty mixture at 50% Lasso and the data fixed.

logistic.title: How does a score become a probability?
logistic.label: Signal coefficient
logistic.help: The coefficient multiplies the same customer signal. The probability conversion is curved, so doubling the score does not double the probability.
logistic.fixed: Keep the signal at about 1.099 and the observed cancellation label at 1.

logistic.title: Does a more confident correct prediction reduce loss?
logistic.label: Signal coefficient
logistic.help: Log loss measures the cost of assigning little probability to the observed outcome. Compare the probabilities and loss for the same customer.
logistic.fixed: Keep the customer and observed label 1 fixed.

logistic.title: When should a probability trigger an action?
logistic.label: Decision threshold
logistic.help: Predict cancellation when its probability reaches the threshold. Raising the threshold changes actions, not the probabilities or fitted model.
logistic.fixed: Keep all customer probabilities, labels and costs fixed.

logistic.title: What does regularization change?
logistic.label: Inverse penalty strength (C)
logistic.help: Smaller C means a stronger coefficient penalty. Compare fitted probabilities without changing the training rows.
logistic.fixed: Use the same fitting workflow and the same development customer.

logistic.title: How does the cost of a missed cancellation change?
logistic.label: Cost of a missed cancellation
logistic.help: Changing a mistake cost changes the cost calculation. It does not refit probabilities or automatically change the decision threshold.
logistic.fixed: Keep the probabilities, labels, threshold 0.5 and false-alarm cost 1 fixed.

logistic.title: Can a good score hide expensive mistakes?
logistic.label: Cost of a missed cancellation
logistic.help: Changing a mistake cost changes the cost calculation. It does not refit probabilities or automatically change the decision threshold.
logistic.fixed: Keep the probabilities, labels, threshold 0.5 and false-alarm cost 1 fixed.

knn.title: Can several neighbours overrule the nearest one?
knn.label: Neighbours consulted (k)
knn.help: KNN finds similar past customers, then lets their labels vote. k is how many neighbours get a vote.
knn.fixed: Keep the customer, distances and equal voting weights fixed.

knn.title: Do measurement units change who looks close?
knn.label: Put measurements on comparable scales
knn.help: A feature measured in large numbers can dominate distance. Scaling changes how distances are calculated, not the customer labels.
knn.fixed: Keep the customer, training rows and k=3 fixed.

knn.title: Does consulting more neighbours help with noise?
knn.label: Neighbours consulted (k)
knn.help: Compare the votes in the same noisy sample. Neither a very small nor a very large k is guaranteed to work best on new customers.
knn.fixed: Keep the noisy sample and query fixed.

knn.title: Can a new customer get a different vote?
knn.label: Customer to predict
knn.help: Each query is a new customer. The training examples and scaling stay fixed; only the customer being predicted changes.
knn.fixed: Keep k=3, training-only scaling and equal vote weights fixed.

naive-bayes.title: How does a starting belief affect a prediction?
naive-bayes.label: Starting class probabilities
naive-bayes.help: A prior is the class probability before reading the document. Compare the training class balance with a supplied 70% prior for the Good class.
naive-bayes.fixed: Keep the same document, word counts and smoothing 0.5.

naive-bayes.title: How can smoothing handle rare words?
naive-bayes.label: Smoothing strength (alpha)
naive-bayes.help: Smoothing adds a small amount to word counts so an unseen word need not erase all support for a class.
naive-bayes.fixed: Keep the document and class prior fixed.

naive-bayes.title: How do numeric measurements become class evidence?
naive-bayes.label: Variance smoothing
naive-bayes.help: Gaussian Naive Bayes describes each class using a mean and spread. Variance smoothing stabilises very small spreads; it can also change the prediction.
naive-bayes.fixed: Keep the numeric observation, features and class prior fixed.

naive-bayes.title: Can repeated evidence create false confidence?
naive-bayes.label: Include a copied measurement
naive-bayes.help: A copied feature repeats information. Naive Bayes can count it again because it treats features as conditionally independent.
naive-bayes.fixed: Keep the same observation, class prior and smoothing.

svm.title: What happens when a decision boundary moves?
svm.label: Boundary position
svm.help: A boundary separates the two predicted classes. Moving its intercept changes which side some points fall on. These supplied boundaries are illustrations, not refitted models.
svm.fixed: Keep the points and boundary direction fixed.

options.label: Move the boundary to the right

svm.title: How much should the model resist training mistakes?
svm.label: Mistake penalty (C)
svm.help: A larger C penalises training margin violations more strongly. Compare the boundary and support points rather than assuming a perfect fit.
svm.fixed: Keep the same noisy points and linear kernel.

svm.title: How local should an RBF boundary be?
svm.label: Influence locality (gamma)
svm.help: RBF compares similarity by distance. Larger gamma makes each point’s influence more local and may create a more intricate boundary.
svm.fixed: Keep C=1, the training points and training-only scaling fixed.

svm.title: Why scale features before comparing distances?
svm.label: Feature scaling
svm.help: Scaling learns means and spreads from training rows. It changes the distances seen by the RBF model.
svm.fixed: Keep the points, C=1 and gamma=1 fixed.

svm.title: Does fitting training points more strongly guarantee reliability?
svm.label: Mistake penalty (C)
svm.help: A stronger training penalty can change the boundary. It does not establish accuracy for future customers or a causal relationship.
svm.fixed: Keep the same noisy points and linear model family.

decision-trees.title: How does one question divide the data?
decision-trees.label: Split threshold
decision-trees.help: Send values at or below the threshold left; send larger values right. Each resulting group supplies its own prediction. This tests a supplied split, not a claim it is the best split.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the rows and the first input feature fixed.

decision-trees.title: What changes when the tree can ask more questions?
decision-trees.label: Maximum tree depth
decision-trees.help: Depth limits the number of decisions along a path. A deeper tree can make finer groups, but may follow noise.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the rows, fitting procedure and minimum leaf size 1 fixed.

decision-trees.title: How does one question divide the data?
decision-trees.label: Split threshold
decision-trees.help: Send values at or below the threshold left; send larger values right. Each resulting group supplies its own prediction. This tests a supplied split, not a claim it is the best split.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the rows and the first input feature fixed.

decision-trees.title: What changes when the tree can ask more questions?
decision-trees.label: Maximum tree depth
decision-trees.help: Depth limits the number of decisions along a path. A deeper tree can make finer groups, but may follow noise.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the rows, fitting procedure and minimum leaf size 1 fixed.

decision-trees.title: Should a leaf be allowed to rely on one example?
decision-trees.label: Minimum examples in a leaf
decision-trees.help: Larger leaves must combine more observations. Compare the predictions without confusing a small training error with future reliability.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the same training data and maximum depth 2.

decision-trees.title: What changes when the tree can ask more questions?
decision-trees.label: Maximum tree depth
decision-trees.help: Depth limits the number of decisions along a path. A deeper tree can make finer groups, but may follow noise.
decision-trees.fixed: Keep the rows, fitting procedure and minimum leaf size 1 fixed.

random-forests.title: What changes when several trees combine predictions?
random-forests.label: Number of trees
random-forests.help: A forest averages regression predictions or class probabilities from different trees. More trees do not guarantee better predictions on every new row.
random-forests.fixed: Keep the data, depth 1, one candidate feature per split and random seed fixed.

random-forests.title: What changes when several trees combine predictions?
random-forests.label: Number of trees
random-forests.help: A forest averages regression predictions or class probabilities from different trees. More trees do not guarantee better predictions on every new row.
random-forests.fixed: Keep the data, depth 1, one candidate feature per split and random seed fixed.

random-forests.title: What changes when several trees combine predictions?
random-forests.label: Number of trees
random-forests.help: A forest averages regression predictions or class probabilities from different trees. More trees do not guarantee better predictions on every new row.
random-forests.fixed: Keep the data, depth 1, one candidate feature per split and random seed fixed.

random-forests.title: What changes when several trees combine predictions?
random-forests.label: Number of trees
random-forests.help: A forest averages regression predictions or class probabilities from different trees. More trees do not guarantee better predictions on every new row.
random-forests.fixed: Keep the data, depth 1, one candidate feature per split and random seed fixed.

random-forests.title: Does changing candidate features change the forest?
random-forests.label: Features considered at each split
random-forests.help: Randomly offering fewer features makes trees explore different questions. Feature importance describes this fitted model, not real-world causation.
random-forests.fixed: Keep three trees, depth 2, the data and random seed fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: Can another small correction improve the prediction?
gradient-boosting.label: Number of correction stages
gradient-boosting.help: Boosting adds trees in sequence. Compare training and development loss; more stages can reduce training loss without improving new-data performance.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and learning rate 0.1 fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: How much of each correction should we apply?
gradient-boosting.label: Learning rate
gradient-boosting.help: Each tree proposes a correction to the current model. The learning rate scales that correction before it is added.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and two correction stages fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: Can another small correction improve the prediction?
gradient-boosting.label: Number of correction stages
gradient-boosting.help: Boosting adds trees in sequence. Compare training and development loss; more stages can reduce training loss without improving new-data performance.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and learning rate 0.1 fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: Can another small correction improve the prediction?
gradient-boosting.label: Number of correction stages
gradient-boosting.help: Boosting adds trees in sequence. Compare training and development loss; more stages can reduce training loss without improving new-data performance.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and learning rate 0.1 fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: Can another small correction improve the prediction?
gradient-boosting.label: Number of correction stages
gradient-boosting.help: Boosting adds trees in sequence. Compare training and development loss; more stages can reduce training loss without improving new-data performance.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and learning rate 0.1 fixed.

gradient-boosting.title: Can another small correction improve the prediction?
gradient-boosting.label: Number of correction stages
gradient-boosting.help: Boosting adds trees in sequence. Compare training and development loss; more stages can reduce training loss without improving new-data performance.
gradient-boosting.fixed: Keep the data, tree settings and learning rate 0.1 fixed.

mlp.title: What does an activation change?
mlp.label: Hidden-unit activation
mlp.help: An activation transforms a weighted sum before the next layer uses it. ReLU keeps positive sums and replaces negative ones with zero. These are supplied weights, not new training.
mlp.fixed: Keep one hidden unit, the input and weights fixed.

options.label: Pass the weighted sum through unchanged
Apply ReLU: replace negative sums with zero

mlp.title: How big should one learning step be?
mlp.label: Learning rate
mlp.help: The learning rate scales the gradient update. A bigger step need not reduce loss more; it can overshoot.
mlp.fixed: Keep the starting weights, observation, logistic activation and zero penalty fixed.

mlp.title: What does a wider hidden layer add?
mlp.label: Hidden-layer width
mlp.help: Each hidden unit computes its own transformed weighted sum. Adding a unit increases capacity; it does not guarantee a better model. The supplied network weights also differ between these examples.
mlp.fixed: Keep the same input and ReLU activation; compare two supplied architectures, not a one-weight intervention.

mlp.title: Should training continue?
mlp.label: Training duration
mlp.help: An epoch is one pass through training data. Compare training and validation loss before deciding which checkpoint to keep.
mlp.fixed: Keep the data, activation, learning rate 0.05 and penalty zero fixed.

mlp.title: Can a penalty help a network generalise?
mlp.label: Coefficient penalty
mlp.help: A penalty discourages large weights. Compare validation results; smaller weights alone do not prove a better future model.
mlp.fixed: Keep the data, ReLU activation, learning rate 0.05 and 32 epochs fixed.

module.title: Could this input be known when we predict?
module.label: When the feature becomes available
module.help: Future information can make an evaluation look excellent while making the model unusable at prediction time.
module.fixed: Keep the housing rows and holdout split fixed.

options.label: Use information available at prediction time
Use information recorded after the prediction

module.title: Are we evaluating on genuinely separate examples?
module.label: Evaluation split
module.help: If the same rows appear in both sets, the validation score no longer measures performance on unfamiliar examples.
module.fixed: Keep the housing data and available features fixed.

options.label: Reuse rows across training and validation

module.title: How does a threshold turn scores into decisions?
module.label: Decision threshold
module.help: A higher threshold requires more confidence before predicting the positive class. Probabilities and ranking stay fixed; decisions and mistake counts may change.
module.fixed: Use the same balanced set of observed labels and supplied probabilities.

module.title: How does a threshold turn scores into decisions?
module.label: Decision threshold
module.help: A higher threshold requires more confidence before predicting the positive class. Probabilities and ranking stay fixed; decisions and mistake counts may change.
module.fixed: Use the same balanced set of observed labels and supplied probabilities.

module.title: Can a model fit too little or too much?
module.label: Model flexibility
module.help: Compare training and development errors. Too little flexibility may miss a pattern; too much may follow noise.
module.fixed: Keep the data and development-based selection rule fixed.

module.title: Could this input be known when we predict?
module.label: When the feature becomes available
module.help: Future information can make an evaluation look excellent while making the model unusable at prediction time.
module.fixed: Keep the housing rows and holdout split fixed.

options.label: Use information available at prediction time
Use information recorded after the prediction

model-selection.title: Does the model improve on a simple baseline?
model-selection.label: Prediction rule
model-selection.help: A baseline is a simple rule to beat. Compare the same validation rows with the same error metric.
model-selection.fixed: Keep the housing task and declared evaluation rows fixed.

model-selection.title: Does extra flexibility help on the same validation houses?
model-selection.label: Model family
model-selection.help: Compare a straight-line model with one that includes squared and interaction inputs. Read the validation result, not just the training fit.
model-selection.fixed: Keep the prediction task and evaluation rows fixed; model capacity changes.

model-selection.title: Are these two scores comparable?
model-selection.label: Rows being compared
model-selection.help: Two scores cannot fairly rank models when they use different examples. A matching row count is not enough.
model-selection.fixed: Keep the regression task and scoring objective fixed.

options.label: Compare scores from different validation rows

model-selection.title: Which data may guide a decision threshold?
model-selection.label: Information used for selection
model-selection.help: Development results guide choices. Final-test data should estimate performance after choices are frozen.
model-selection.fixed: Compare selection policies; this is a workflow contrast, not a fitted parameter change.

options.label: Choose the threshold using development data

model-selection.title: Can related examples leak across the split?
model-selection.label: Group separation
model-selection.help: Different rows can still describe the same customer or group. Keeping groups separate tests transfer to unfamiliar groups.
model-selection.fixed: Compare validation policies on the declared grouped task; no test targets are exposed.

options.label: Let related groups appear on both sides

model-selection.title: When is it time to open the final test?
model-selection.label: Workflow stage
model-selection.help: Development is for choosing. The final test is for a one-time evaluation of a frozen choice, not another tuning round.
model-selection.fixed: No final-test targets or scores are shown in this playground.
